Baseline report · Chapters 01 to 24

Seal Bay

How guests move around a seaside holiday resort on the West Sussex coast, and what that means for walking and wheeling between caravans, attractions and places to eat.

Spatial Design Hub and Momentum Transport Consultancy, working together.

Scroll to begin
01

Seal Bay and surroundings

Seal Bay is a seaside holiday resort on the south coast of West Sussex, just west of Selsey. Its location places the resort close to the town, while the wider area’s main urban centres are located further away.

Bognor Regis and Chichester are each around a 30-minute drive from Seal Bay, while Portsmouth is approximately 40 minutes away. These journey times are indicative and may vary depending on traffic and the time of year.

The nearest railway stations are Chichester and Bognor Regis. Visitors travelling by rail will therefore need to make an onward journey from the station to reach Seal Bay.

The 51 bus provides a public transport connection between Seal Bay, Selsey and Chichester. It runs to Selsey around three times per hour, with services continuing to Seal Bay around once per hour and stopping by the Windmill. This offers a link to the resort for visitors and residents without a car, though services to Seal Bay are less frequent than those to Selsey.

02

Seal Bay’s internal areas

Seal Bay is made up of four distinct areas:

  • West Sands
  • Warner Farm Touring Park
  • White Horse
  • Green Lawns

The areas are connected by the resort’s internal roads, most notably Warner’s Lane, which runs from Green Lawns down to West Sands, but the connections can be difficult to navigate by walking or wheeling.

Hover over an area on the map to see its size.

03

Seal Bay’s internal network

The map presents Seal Bay’s existing internal network, distinguishing between intersite connections, shared pedestrian and vehicle routes, and dedicated footpaths. It also identifies bus stops, micromobility hubs and one-way road arrangements, alongside potential points of severance and missing links.

Much of the network within the accommodation areas is shared with vehicles, while dedicated footpaths provide alternatives in some locations, including around the perimeter of West Sands.

The indicative severance points highlight locations where gaps or discontinuities may interrupt otherwise connected routes. Alongside the potential missing links, these identify areas for further investigation to establish how walking and wheeling connections could be made more continuous and better integrated with the resort’s bus service and cycle hire provision.

The glowing blue dashes are potential missing links. Hover over one to see how much shorter the journey would be compared with today’s route.

04

Seal Bay’s connectivity

This map uses a Movement Connectivity Analysis to assess how well connected the movement network is across the parks. Rather than simply showing where routes exist, the analysis considers how each route connects to the wider network, identifying those that are more important for movement across the site.

The most connected routes (red and orange) form the main corridors linking different areas and facilities, while less connected roads and cul-de-sacs (blue and purple) primarily serve local access.

Many of the most connected routes are shared by pedestrians and vehicles, meaning guests are often directed onto the same roads as traffic. The analysis helps identify where movement is likely to be concentrated, where alternative routes are limited, and where improvements to the network could have the greatest impact on connectivity and pedestrian accessibility.

The map indicates that the core roads across the site, such as Warner’s Lane, Nab Tower Lane and Deer Park Lane, are well connected, as shown by the high connectivity score. However, the lower connectivity scores between these core roads suggest a lack of continuity across the site.

Hover over a street to see its connectivity band.

05

Seal Bay’s accessibility

Seal Bay’s facilities and points of interest are spread across the site, but are most concentrated at West Sands, with further clusters at White Horse and Green Lawns. The mapped accessibility scores therefore vary across the accommodation areas, reflecting how close guests are to key amenities and destinations.

There are three key ‘transport deserts’ located across the sites, which can be found to the south-west of West Sands, the north-west of White Horse, and the north of Green Lawns. These areas currently do not have footways and therefore restrict accessibility to points of interest.

Low scores can also be found at the northern edge of West Sands, near Warner Farm; the western side of White Horse; and the northern edge of Green Lawns. These areas are furthest from the main clusters of facilities, so guests staying there may need to travel further to reach attractions and services.

Improving connections from these transport deserts and lower-accessibility areas could help make the resort’s amenities easier to reach on foot or by wheeling.

Hover over a hexagon to see walking times from it to each type of destination. Select an icon to list the venues there.

06

Walking connectivity

This analysis explores how easily guests can reach key attractions and bus stops across Seal Bay, highlighting patterns of connectivity between accommodation areas, facilities and the internal transport network.

Walking routes are assessed along the park’s existing road and path network, using different walking speeds to reflect the mobility of the guest groups represented in the simulated population. A five-minute walking threshold is used to examine the relative accessibility of key destinations, with overlapping routes helping to illustrate how connections are distributed across the site and whether bus stops or attractions are more easily reached.

The results highlight differences in walking accessibility across the parks, identifying well-connected areas, more isolated parts of the network and locations where the bus service may provide a useful alternative to walking. These patterns help inform opportunities to improve pedestrian connections, strengthen access to facilities and review the coverage of the internal bus service.

Hover over a route to see how many caravan routes use it.

07

Site visit findings

Momentum visited Seal Bay on 13 October to observe how people move around the resort and identify key transport-related constraints and opportunities.

The main issue observed was the discontinuous pedestrian network. Footways stop abruptly in several places, with the most significant gap along Warner’s Lane between the reception area and White Horse/Green Lawns. This section has no footway and a ditch runs alongside the carriageway. As a busy link between the resort’s different areas, as demonstrated by the Movement Connectivity Analysis, it can make journeys on foot or by wheelchair difficult and uncomfortable. The lack of street lighting may make conditions more challenging after dark.

There are also existing options that support movement around the site. The internal bus service connects key areas and is reported to be well used during the summer peak. App-based cycle hire offers another way to travel, while the nature footpath around West Sands provides a vehicle-free alternative for some journeys. These services and routes offer a foundation for a more connected and accessible travel network.

Select a photo or a pin to see it larger.

08

Who is visiting?

During the site visit, Seal Bay’s Facilities Management team provided a high-level estimate of the resort’s typical guest profile during the summer peak, which falls during the July and August school holidays. They estimated that around 90% of guests are families with children, with most of the remaining visitors being older couples aged 60 or over.

For the purposes of this assessment, we have represented visitors using these two broad groups: families with children and older couples. This provides a practical basis for considering how different guests may use the resort and what journeys they are likely to make between their accommodation and key destinations.

The proportions are indicative rather than the result of a detailed visitor survey, and the mix of guests may vary at other times of year. To simplify the analysis, the remaining 10% of summer visitors are treated as older couples.

09

Why, when and between which places?

This section explores how families with children and older couples may move around Seal Bay, using indicative ‘day in the life’ itineraries for guests staying in different areas. Daytime and night-time journeys are considered separately to understand connections between accommodation, attractions, places to eat and evening venues.

For each group, existing routes show how these journeys can be made using the current network. Desire line routes show more direct connections between destinations, including potential informal cut-throughs between caravans. They reflect where guests may want to travel, regardless of the surface or traffic conditions along the way, rather than confirmed routes taken by visitors.

Comparing the two helps identify where new connections could make journeys more direct, and where existing routes already follow the desired alignment but could be made more comfortable for walking and wheeling.

10

Families with children

The itineraries presented here provide an indicative ‘day in the life’ for a family with children during the peak summer season, starting from the area where they are staying. They are based on the resort’s main family attractions and places to eat, and assume that families make several trips beyond their accommodation during the day. The times are illustrative rather than a fixed schedule; activities and movements will vary between guests and with the season.

The assumed destinations vary by accommodation area:

  • West Sands, Warner Farm or Hollyhocks: Crazy Golf, Box Lunch and the Fun Fair, followed by Selby’s in the evening.
  • White Horse: the Arcade, Box Lunch and the Lido, followed by Smokey’s.
  • Green Lawns: outdoor activities, Papa John’s and the beach, followed by The Viking.

Together, these itineraries help identify likely routes between accommodation, daytime attractions, places to eat and evening venues, which are explored on the following slides.

Select an itinerary to label its stops on the map. Select it again to clear.

11

Families with children: existing day routes

Daytime · 10am – 2pm

The map shows the most direct routes implied by the daytime itineraries, linking each family’s accommodation area with the activities and destinations they are assumed to visit. These are indicative desire lines applied to the existing network rather than confirmed routes taken by guests.

Warner’s Lane is the main connection between the resort’s different areas and is likely to be used by families travelling between West Sands, White Horse and Green Lawns. Within West Sands, routes also use West Sands Lane to reach the Fun Fair and nearby attractions. Families travelling from Green Lawns towards destinations in White Horse are likely to use Goldfinch Way. This suggests that a small number of internal routes may carry much of the movement between accommodation and daytime activities.

Walking and bus times are those given in the report. Hover over a route to see its stops.

12

Families with children: desire line day routes

Daytime · 10am – 2pm

The daytime desire lines broadly follow the existing routes, suggesting that the main connections between family attractions remain important. However, differences emerge closer to accommodation in West Sands and White Horse, where more direct journeys would pass between caravans rather than follow the surrounding roads.

In southern West Sands, the desire lines also use connections between caravans and Coral Lane to join the north-eastern section of Warner’s Lane, rather than following Warner’s Lane for the full journey towards White Horse and Green Lawns. These differences highlight potential opportunities for more direct walking and wheeling links, subject to assessing the space available and their suitability.

Walking and bus times are those given in the report. Hover over a route to see its stops.

13

Families with children: existing night routes

Evening · 6pm – late

The night-time routes show families travelling from their accommodation to evening venues, including Selby’s, Smokey’s and The Viking, before returning to their caravan. As during the day, Warner’s Lane forms an important link between West Sands and the eastern parts of the resort. Routes within West Sands connect accommodation with evening venues, while families staying in Green Lawns are shown travelling to The Viking.

These journeys highlight the importance of comfortable, legible routes for families returning to their accommodation after dark. In particular, the section of Warner’s Lane between the reception area and White Horse/Green Lawns has no footway or street lighting, which may make walking or wheeling along this key connection feel difficult and uncomfortable at night.

Walking and bus times are those given in the report. Hover over a route to see its stops.

14

Families with children: desire line night routes

Evening · 6pm – late

The night-time desire lines retain many of the existing connections to evening venues but show opportunities to shorten journeys to and from accommodation. As in the daytime, routes in West Sands and White Horse veer between caravans, indicating where the existing network does not currently facilitate these journeys.

Connections through southern West Sands and via Coral Lane provide a more direct alignment towards the north-eastern section of Warner’s Lane. These potential links could help families return to their accommodation more easily, but directness alone would not make them suitable after dark. Any new route would also need an appropriate surface, clear wayfinding and consideration of lighting.

Walking and bus times are those given in the report. Hover over a route to see its stops.

15

Older couples

The itineraries presented here provide an indicative ‘day in the life’ for an older couple, starting from the area where they are staying. They reflect a relatively relaxed pattern of activity, including visits to the beach, places to eat and other on-site facilities. The times are illustrative rather than a fixed schedule, and individual plans will vary.

The assumed destinations vary by accommodation area:

  • West Sands, Warner Farm or Hollyhocks: the beach, lunch at Box Lunch and the Oasis Pool, followed by an evening at their caravan.
  • White Horse: the Pottery Studio, Café Lido and the beach, followed by Smokey’s in the evening.
  • Green Lawns: the beach, lunch at Box Lunch and the Pottery Studio, followed by The Viking in the evening.

Together, these itineraries help indicate the journeys older couples may make between their accommodation and key destinations, which are explored on the following slides.

Select an itinerary to label its stops on the map. Select it again to clear.

16

Older couples: existing day routes

Daytime · 10am – 2pm

This map shows the most direct routes implied by the older-couple daytime itineraries, linking accommodation areas with destinations such as the beach, Box Lunch, the Oasis Pool and the Pottery Studio. These are indicative desire lines based on the assumed ‘day in the life’, rather than confirmed routes taken by guests.

As with the family itineraries, Warner’s Lane is an important link for journeys between the different parts of the resort. Goldfinch Way also appears in routes to and from the Green Lawns area. In contrast, West Sands Lane is not expected to carry the same level of movement for this user group, as it primarily provides access to the Fun Fair, which is more likely to feature in family journeys.

Walking and bus times are those given in the report. Hover over a route to see its stops.

17

Older couples: desire line day routes

Daytime · 10am – 2pm

The daytime desire lines retain Warner’s Lane as an important connection between West Sands and the eastern areas but differ from existing routes within the accommodation areas. In southern West Sands, they pass between caravans and use Coral Lane to reach the north-eastern section of Warner’s Lane, avoiding the need to follow its full alignment.

Some desire lines also pass between caravans in White Horse, highlighting opportunities to shorten connections between accommodation and nearby destinations. These alignments indicate where new or upgraded paths could reduce indirect journeys, provided they can offer a continuous, comfortable route for walking and wheeling.

Walking and bus times are those given in the report. Hover over a route to see its stops.

18

Older couples: existing night routes

Evening · 6pm – late

The nighttime map shows the assumed evening journeys for older couples, including trips to Smokey’s and The Viking, followed by a return to their accommodation. The routes indicate that Warner’s Lane remains an important connection between West Sands and the eastern parts of the resort, while Goldfinch Way provides access to destinations within the eastern areas.

These routes suggest that journeys between accommodation and evening venues may rely on the same internal connections used during the day.

Walking and bus times are those given in the report. Hover over a route to see its stops.

19

Older couples: desire line night routes

Evening · 6pm – late

The night-time desire lines show a similar pattern to those identified during the day. While the main connections to evening venues remain important, more direct journeys would use links between caravans in southern West Sands and White Horse, including a connection via Coral Lane towards Warner’s Lane.

This suggests that the same local connections could support both daytime and evening travel. Alongside opportunities to shorten journeys, the comparison highlights the importance of route quality: potential cut-throughs would need suitable surfaces, legible connections and consideration of lighting to provide a comfortable alternative after dark.

Walking and bus times are those given in the report. Hover over a route to see its stops.

20

All users: existing routes

This map combines the indicative routes for families with children and older couples across both daytime and nighttime to show where journeys overlap. Routes are grouped by how many of the modelled journeys use them: key shared corridors carry the greatest overlap, while other routes are shared by several journeys or appear in only one.

Warner’s Lane stands out as a key shared corridor, connecting West Sands with White Horse and Green Lawns across both user groups and different times of day. Routes through White Horse and via Goldfinch Way are shared by several journeys.

Hover over a corridor to see how many modelled journeys use it.

21

All users: desire line routes

Combining the desire lines for both user groups across daytime and nighttime highlights the clearest opportunities to improve directness. The main differences from the existing network occur around Coral Lane in West Sands and between caravans in White Horse, where several journeys would benefit from connections that avoid following less direct road layouts.

These areas could be investigated for new or upgraded walking and wheeling links, subject to space, access and feasibility checks. Where desire lines and existing routes already align, particularly along the remaining sections of Warner’s Lane, the priority is instead to improve the quality and continuity of the existing route. Together, these approaches would support a network that is both more direct and more comfortable to use.
